extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, students, and practitioners interested in esports
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey of esports covering history, game design, competition formats, governance, viewership, and policy issues. The page summarizes facts and recurring evaluative points used when judging or organizing esports (e.g., whether something counts as a sport; how to design spectator features; integrity concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification as a sport
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling competitive video games as a sport is controversial; proponents argue esports require 'careful planning, precise timing, and skillful execution' while opponents claim sports involve physical fitness and physical training. The IOC has noted concerns about violent games and the lack of a global sanctioning body and stated that competitive 'esports' could be considered a sporting activity if games fit 'with the rules and regulations of the Olympic movement'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria used in arguments and policy decisions include: whether the game involves physical training/fitness or is primarily mental; whether the game's content (e.g., violent themes) aligns with Olympic values; whether there is a recognized governing/sanctioning body; and whether the game can be mapped to sports-simulating activities that promote good physical and mental health (or VR/AR games that include physical activity). Examples of national/regulatory recognition (Russia, China, Turkey, etc.) and IOC positions are cited as part of the evaluative framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game design suitability for professional competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Many successful esports games have been designed to be played professionally from the beginning. Developers may add dedicated esports features or make design compromises to support high-level competition (examples cited: StarCraft II, League of Legends, Dota 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design decisions that indicate esports suitability include built-in competitive balance, support for tournaments, matchmaking for ranked play, and features aimed at professional play. The page cites these design choices as factors that make a game more likely to become a successful esport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectator mode / observability
rubrics_metrics.description: Games often include dedicated observing features for spectators, ranging from simple player POV to highly modified interfaces that give spectators access to information even the players may not have. Spectator features are common in esports titles (Counter-Strike series, Call of Duty, StarCraft II, Dota 2, League of Legends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practices noted include providing clear spectator interfaces, possibly augmented information for viewers, and implementing broadcast delays to prevent teams from gaining a competitive advantage. The page notes some games added VR spectating support (Dota 2) as technology evolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online competition considerations (latency, cheating, matchmaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online play is a very common connection method; downsides include increased difficulty detecting cheating and greater network latency which can negatively impact player performance. Game servers are often separated by region, with automated matchmaking clients built into many games (e.g., Battle.net, Xbox Live, PlayStation Network).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers should account for latency (regional servers, quality-of-service) and invest in anti-cheat/detection systems for online events. Automated matchmaking and server infrastructure are cited as central components; examples emphasize that many smaller tournaments and exhibition matches take place online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local area network (LAN) for fair play and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitions are often conducted over a LAN which usually has very little lag and higher quality. Because competitors must be physically present, LANs help ensure fair play by allowing direct scrutiny and preventing hardware/software modding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major tournaments are typically held on LAN to ensure integrity and spectator quality. The page cites negative reactions when popular competitive titles (e.g., StarCraft II at release) lacked LAN support, illustrating the expectation that top-level events use LAN settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tournament formats and league organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Esports uses many tournament formats including series of league play with sponsored teams, standalone major tournaments (e.g., League of Legends World Championship, Dota 2's The International), and genre-specific circuits (EVO for fighting games).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When organizing or evaluating events, considerations include format (league vs. single-event), sponsorship and team structures, rotation of venues, prize pool distribution, and whether the event is publisher-run or independent. The page discusses proliferation of tournaments and experimentation with formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize pools and funding models
rubrics_metrics.description: Prize pools in esports can be very large (e.g., Dota 2's The International funded via Compendium/battle pass), but financial security is largely limited to players in top performing teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of an ecosystem's health looks at how prize money is funded (publisher support, crowd-funded battle passes, sponsorships), salary structures, and whether teams provide stable support (salaries, travel expenses). The page notes that only a minority of professionals enjoy long careers and stable income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Player professionalization, licensing, and legal recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments and organizations have at times formally recognized esports players as professionals (examples: China recognized esports players as an occupation; Turkey and the Philippines issuing esports licenses; a P-1A visa for a pro gamer in the U.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for national recognition include licensing schemes, visa categories for athletes, official profession designation, and creation of national associations. These legal/regulatory tools are used to evaluate and enable professional careers in esports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training regimens and athlete welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Esports athletes often have extensive training routines (example: Team Liquid's League of Legends team practices a minimum of 50 hours per week). Researchers found some top players show aspects of mental toughness similar to Olympic athletes, though careers can be short and early retirement is common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of players/teams consider practice volume, coaching, mental/physical health support, and career longevity. Organizers and teams should consider athlete welfare given long practice hours and short professional windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity and anti-cheating measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheating is a recurring issue: online competition increases difficulty of detecting cheating compared to physical events; LAN presence helps prevent unauthorized hardware/software modding. The article also references integrity organizations and regulatory concerns in lists of bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended measures include physical scrutiny at LAN events, robust anti-cheat software and enforcement online, regulation via integrity bodies, and policies around betting/sponsorship to reduce conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre suitability and competitive viability
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain video game genres are most commonly associated with esports: MOBA, FPS, fighting games, card games, battle royales, and RTS. Popular esports franchises are listed (League of Legends, Dota, Counter-Strike, Valorant, Overwatch, Street Fighter, Super Smash Bros., StarCraft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a game's potential as an esport, consider genre characteristics that support competition (direct player-vs-player competition, spectator clarity, balance, depth for high-skill play) and whether developers support competitive features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting and streaming as core distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The advent of online streaming platforms (YouTube, Twitch) enabled a surge in professional participation and viewership; Twitch and other platforms are the most common methods of watching tournaments and are central to audience growth and monetization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful events and leagues prioritize streaming/broadcast infrastructure, partnership deals (example: Riot's broadcast contracts), and content suitable for both live and archived viewing. Viewer metrics and platform partnerships are key evaluative dimensions for event success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and policy constraints affecting events
rubrics_metrics.description: National laws and policies (e.g., Japan's anti-gambling laws limiting paid professional gaming tournaments; China's restrictions on minors' playtime; state betting regulations) materially affect how esports can be run and recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers and evaluators must account for local legal restrictions on gambling, age restrictions, licensing requirements, and regulatory recognition; mitigation strategies include obtaining exemptions, designing events to comply with local law, or shifting venues (as in the example of The International being moved).
